text:
Then the joyous cavalcade set out, escorted by the children on foot, who ran along firing pistol shots and making the horses rear. Mother Maurice rode in a little cart with Germain’s three children and the minstrels. They led the procession to the sound of the instruments. Little Pierre was so handsome that the old grandmother was very proud of him. But the impetuous child did not remain beside her for long. During a halt that had to be made halfway there in order to enter a difficult passage, he slipped away and went to beg his father to seat him in front of him on the _Gray Mare_.

“Indeed!” replied Germain, “that will bring unpleasant jests down on us! We must not.”

“I care little what the people of Saint-Chartier will say,” said little Marie. “Take him, Germain, I beg you: I shall be even prouder of him than of my wedding finery.”

Germain yielded, and the handsome trio dashed through the ranks at the triumphant gallop of the _Gray Mare_.

And indeed, although the people of Saint-Chartier were great mockers and somewhat given to teasing the neighboring parishes that had gathered in theirs, it did not occur to them to laugh when they saw so handsome a bridegroom, so pretty a bride, and a child who would have been the envy of a king’s wife. Little Pierre had a complete suit of cornflower-blue cloth, and a red waistcoat so smart and so short that it scarcely reached below his chin. The village tailor had made the armholes so tight that he could not bring his two little arms together. And how proud he was! He had a round hat with a black-and-gold band, and a peacock feather jutting boldly from a tuft of guinea-fowl feathers. A bouquet of flowers larger than his head covered his shoulder, and its ribbons floated down to his feet. The hemp-dresser, who was also the local barber and wigmaker, had cut his hair in a circle by covering his head with a bowl and trimming off everything that protruded, an infallible method for ensuring an even cut. Dressed up in this fashion, the poor child was assuredly less poetic than with his long hair blowing in the wind and his sheepskin in the manner of Saint John the Baptist; but he did not think so, and everyone admired him, saying that he looked like a little man. His beauty triumphed over everything; and over what, indeed, would the incomparable beauty of childhood not triumph?

His little sister Solange wore, for the first time in her life, a bonnet instead of the printed-cotton cap worn by little girls until the age of two or three. And what a bonnet! Taller and broader than the poor little thing’s whole body. And how beautiful she thought herself! She did not dare turn her head and held herself perfectly stiff, thinking that people would take her for the bride.

As for little Sylvain, he was still in a gown, and, asleep on his grandmother’s lap, he had scarcely any notion of what a wedding was.

Germain looked lovingly at his children, and upon arriving at the town hall, he said to his betrothed:

“Look, Marie, I arrive here a little happier than on the day when I brought you home from the woods of Chanteloube, believing that you would never love me; I took you in my arms to set you on the ground, just as I do now; but I thought that we would never again find ourselves together on the poor good Gray Mare with this child on our knees. Look, I love you so much, I love these poor little ones so much, I am so happy that you love me, and that you love them, and that my parents love you, and I love your mother and my friends and everyone so much today that I wish I had three or four hearts to hold it all. Truly, one is too little to house so much affection and so much happiness! It almost gives me a pain in my stomach.”

There was a crowd at the doors of the town hall and the church to look at the pretty bride. Why should we not describe her attire? It suited her so well! Her bonnet of sheer muslin, embroidered all over, had lappets trimmed with _rientelle_ lace. In those days peasant women did not permit themselves to show a single hair; and although beneath their bonnets they conceal magnificent heads of hair wound in white cotton ribbons to support the headdress, even today it would be considered indecent and shameful to appear before men bareheaded. Nevertheless, they now permit themselves to leave a narrow band of hair visible across the forehead, which greatly enhances their beauty. But I regret the classical headdress of my day: that white lace lying directly against the skin possessed a quality of ancient chastity that seemed to me more solemn, and when a face was beautiful framed in that way, its beauty had a charm and artless majesty that nothing can express.

Little Marie still wore that headdress, and her forehead was so white and pure that it defied the whiteness of the linen to make it look dark. Although she had not closed her eyes all night, the morning air, and above all the inward joy of a soul as limpid as the sky, together with a little secret ardor, restrained by adolescent modesty, brought to her cheeks a radiance as sweet as peach blossom in the first rays of April.

Her white kerchief, chastely crossed over her breast, revealed only the delicate contours of a neck rounded like a turtledove’s; her jacket of fine myrtle-green cloth outlined her small waist, which seemed perfect but was yet to grow and develop, for she was not seventeen. She wore a pansy-purple silk apron with a bib, which our village women were wrong to do away with and which lent so much elegance and modesty to the bosom. Today they display their kerchiefs with greater pride, but their attire no longer possesses that delicate bloom of ancient chasteness that made them resemble Holbein virgins. They are more coquettish, more graceful. In former times, good style consisted of a kind of severe stiffness that made their rare smiles deeper and more ideal.

At the offertory, Germain placed in his betrothed’s hand, according to custom, the _treizain_, that is, thirteen silver coins. He slipped onto her finger a silver ring, of a form unchanged for centuries, but which has now been replaced by the _gold wedding band_. On leaving the church, Marie said softly to him:

“Is it really the ring I wished for? The one I asked you for, Germain?”

“Yes,” he replied, “the one my Catherine wore on her finger when she died. It is the same ring for both my marriages.”
